newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: S.Pacific Forum opposes PNG's use of mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: S.Pacific Forum opposes PNG's use of mercenaries.

text.p: The Solomon Islands, a canoe ride from strife-torn Bougainville, has condemned Papua New Guinea's use of mercenaries in the island's conflict as "cowardly" and will take its neighbour to the International Court of Justice.
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Solomon Mamaloni called on the 16-nation South Pacific Forum, which includes Australia and New Zealand, to back its legal action against Papua New Guinea.

"The PNG government's introduction of mercenaries into the region is...regarded as a cowardly act and contrary to the enhancement of the 'Pacific way'," Mamaloni said in a statement received here on Wednesday.
"It is a dangerous precedent which will destabilise the peace and harmony within the Forum countries and throw everyone back into the former cannibalism days," Mamaloni said.
"Mercenaries should never be introduced into this region unless Forum leaders are totally incapable of leading their respective governments and nations."
Mamaloni said the case would be lodged in the International Court of Justice in The Hague in late March.

The move also prompted Papua New Guinea's first prime minister, Sir Michael Somare, and eight other independent MPs to call for the resignations of current Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan and Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta.

"This government has gone berserk and its leadership need their brains scanned. This nation is in the very real danger of being governed by madmen," said Somare in a statement from Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea.

The Bougainville conflict began in 1989 when landowners disgruntled with royalty payments from the giant Panguna copper mine in central Bougainville sabotaged the mine. The dispute eventually mushroomed into a full-scale revolt against Papua New Guinea's rule in which hundreds have been killed.
The Solomon Islands, an archipelago covering some 600,000 sq km (230,000 sq miles), is a "victim" of the Bougainville conflict, said Mamaloni.
He said Papua New Guinea troops and government-backed resistance forces have regularly crossed into the Solomon Islands, chasing and engaging rebels, with 40 incursions in 1996.
Papua New Guinea has hired some 40 African mercenaries through British-based Sandline International to train government troops for a mission against Bougainville's rebels.
Australia, New Zealand, Britain, the United States and South Africa have all criticised Papua New Guinea for hiring mercenaries.
Sir Michael Somare is regarded as the father of Papua New Guinea, leading it to independence from Australia in 1975, and has widespread popular support throughout the country.
He said the Chan government had usurped the authority of the parliament and undermined the integrity of the defence force by hiring mercenaries.
"Bougainville cannot be resolved through gun-barrel diplomacy, nor through a bloodbath. Bougainville needs patient and honest dialogue and consultation," he said.
The MPs called on the government to cancel the mercenary plan immediately and deport and "blacklist" any foreigners involved in the scheme.
Chan has said the mercenaries are part of a "radical initiative" to end the nine-year conflict, re-open the Panguna mine, and pay local landowners compensation.
